steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - inverse problems e.g. healthcare: interpretability paramount; hard technically, needs flexible frameworks
  - structure solutions into pipelines; interpretable steps -> interpretable overall model
  - NLP, medical informatics, bioinformatics: high-dimensional count matrices
  - dimensionality reduction -> representations (factors / embeddings) fed downstream
  - goal: dimension reduction for count matrices with innate interpretation in terms of original features
- 1.1 Interpretability vs explainability
  - want not only post-hoc explainable (cite) but intrinsically interpretable (cite)
  - definition: clear how outputs computed from original variables; latent variables + interactions meaningful
  - post-hoc: subjective examination via subject-matter expertise; black-box -> simpler approximating models (local linear regressions); inexact, can mislead (cite)
  - examples throughout deep learning literature
- 1.2 Disentangled autoencoders
  - disentangled VAEs (cite): mindful of post-hoc explainability; encoder-decoder (Definitions 1 and 2)
  - encoder: input features -> latent representations; decoder: latent representations -> predictions
  - penalties (cite) + structural constraints (cite) -> statistical independence
  - from computer vision; conceptually sensible nonlinear factors
  - explanations via local saliency maps unreliable/imprecise (cite)
  - pixels: not needed; structured data: want effects of individual features
- 1.3 Probabilistic matrix factorization
  - related to autoencoders (cite); recommender systems: rows = users, columns (features) = items
  - bi-linear in item- and user-specific effects, like item response theory (cite)
  - non-negative sparse MF: only additive terms (cite)
  - HPF for count matrices (cite): \mathbf{Y}=(y_{ui}) U\times I; Eq. 1; \bm{\Theta}=(\theta_{uk}), \mathbf{B}=(\beta_{ki}) decoder
  - priors \eta_{i}, \xi_{u}; hyper-parameters a^{\prime},b^{\prime},c^{\prime},d^{\prime}
  - \bm{\theta}_{u} K-dimensional representation; \mathbf{B} decodes into predictions
  - gamma priors: non-negativity, sparsity (density at zero)
  - interpretation: prediction = linear combination of subset of representation elements (Fig. 1 a); factor composition not explicit, from Bayesian inference (Fig. 1 c)
- 1.4 Limitations of HPF
  - NMF column-clustering property (cite); HPF of Eq. 1 lacks it
  - encoder (Def. 1) not explicit; decoder rows not enough; sparse decoding =/= sparse encoding (pseudo-inverses)
  - no feature selection: decoder terms near zero iff feature mean near zero; can imply structure in pure Poisson noise (Fig. 3 a)
- 1.5 Contributions
  - self-consistently constrain HPF -> explicit encoder; interpretability + feature selection
  - large datasets: representation matrix not stored in memory
  - medical claims case study: decision rules in representation space -> rules on original features

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
For many inverse problems, for example the ones in healthcare, model interpretability is paramount. It is technically challenging to build interpretable solutions that also perform well, and it needs flexible frameworks. A general approach to these problems and others is to structure the solutions into pipelines. If each step in the pipeline is interpretable, then the overall larger model is interpretable too.

Data sources in natural language processing, medical informatics, and bioinformatics are often high-dimensional count matrices. When modeling high-dimensional data sets, a common first step is dimensionality reduction to find data representations that are tractable (also called factors or embeddings), which are then fed into downstream analyses. Our goal is to develop a dimension reduction scheme for count matrices where the reduced representation has an innate interpretation in terms of the original data features.

## 1.1 Interpretability versus explainability

We want latent data representations which are not only post-hoc explainable, but also intrinsically interpretable. By our definition, intrinsic interpretability requires that it is clear how the outputs of the model are computed from the original variables, and that the latent variables and the interactions inside the model are meaningful.

Post-hoc explanations come from a subjective examination of a solution through the lens of subject-matter expertise. For black-box models without intrinsic interpretability, the explanations are produced with simpler approximating models (typically local linear regressions). The explanations are inexact, and they can also be misleading. Black-box models that rely on approximation techniques for explainability can be found all through the deep learning literature.

## 1.2 Disentangled autoencoders

Disentangled variational autoencoders are deep learning models which are inherently mindful of post-hoc model explainability. Like other autoencoders, they have an encoder-decoder structure (see Definitions 1 and 2), and the encoder generates dimensionally reduced representations.

The encoder transformation maps input data features to latent representations

The decoder transformation maps latent representations to predictions

Disentangled autoencoders use a combination of penalties and structural constraints to encourage statistical independence in the representations, which helps explanation. These methods came from computer vision and have shown empirical utility in producing nonlinear factor models where the factors are conceptually sensible. But because deep learning is a black-box, the explanations of how the factors are generated from the data, using local saliency maps for example, are unreliable or imprecise. In imaging applications the features are raw pixels, and this type of interpretability is not necessary. But when modeling structured data problems, one often wants to learn the effects of the individual data features.

## 1.3 Probabilistic matrix factorization

- related to autoencoders; recommender systems: rows = users, columns (features) = items
- bi-linear in item- and user-specific effects (item response theory); non-negative sparse MF -> additive terms
- HPF for count matrices: \mathbf{Y}=(y_{ui}) U\times I, Eq. 1, \bm{\Theta}=(\theta_{uk}), decoder \mathbf{B}=(\beta_{ki}), priors \eta_{i} and \xi_{u}
- gamma priors: non-negativity + sparsity; prediction = linear combination of subset of representation elements (Fig. 1 a); factor composition from Bayesian inference (Fig. 1 c)

## 1.4 Limitations of HPF

- no column-clustering property like NMF
- no explicit encoder; sparse decoding =/= sparse encoding
- no feature selection; fake structure in pure Poisson noise (Fig. 3 a)

## 1.5 Our contributions

- constrain HPF so encoder explicit; interpretability, feature selection, large datasets
- medical claims case study

For black-box models without intrinsic interpretability, the explanations are produced with simpler approximating models (typically local linear regressions). The explanations are inexact, and they can also be misleading. Black-box models that rely on approximation techniques for explainability can be found all through the deep learning literature.

## 1.2 Disentangled autoencoders

Disentangled variational autoencoders are deep learning models which are inherently mindful of post-hoc model explainability. Like other autoencoders, they have an encoder-decoder structure (see Definitions 1 and 2), and the encoder generates dimensionally reduced representations.

The encoder transformation maps input data features to latent representations

The decoder transformation maps latent representations to predictions

Disentangled autoencoders use a combination of penalties and structural constraints to encourage statistical independence in the representations, which helps explanation. These methods came from computer vision and have shown empirical utility in producing nonlinear factor models where the factors are conceptually sensible. But because deep learning is a black-box, the explanations of how the factors are generated from the data, using local saliency maps for example, are unreliable or imprecise. In imaging applications the features are raw pixels, and this type of interpretability is not necessary. But when modeling structured data problems, one often wants to learn the effects of the individual data features.

## 1.3 Probabilistic matrix factorization

Probabilistic matrix factorization methods are related to autoencoders. They are often presented in the context of recommender systems, where rows of the input matrix are attributed to users and columns (features) are attributed to items. Probabilistic matrix factorization methods are bi-linear in item- and user-specific effects, and they de-convolve them in a similar way to item response theory. When the data is non-negative, non-negative sparse matrix factorization methods improve interpretability further by computing predictions only with additive terms.

For count matrices, previous work introduced hierarchical Poisson matrix factorization (HPF). Suppose \mathbf{Y}=(y_{ui}) is a U\times I matrix of non-negative integers, where each row corresponds to a user and each column corresponds to an item (feature). Using their notation, the HPF authors formulated their model as

where \bm{\Theta}=(\theta_{uk}) is a U\times K matrix, and \mathbf{B}=(\beta_{ki}) is the representation decoder matrix. The additional priors \eta_{i}\sim\textrm{Gamma}(c^{\prime},c^{\prime}/d^{\prime}) and \xi_{u}\sim\textrm{Gamma}(a^{\prime},a^{\prime}/b^{\prime}) model item and user-specific variability in the dataset, and a^{\prime},b^{\prime},c^{\prime},d^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{+} are hyper-parameters. The row vector \bm{\theta}_{u}=(\theta_{u1},\ldots,\theta_{uK}) is a K -dimensional representation of the user, and the matrix \mathbf{B}=(\beta_{ki}) decodes the representation into predictions of the user's counts.

In HPF the gamma priors on the decoder matrix \mathbf{B}=(\beta_{ki}) enforce non-negativity. The gamma distribution can have density at zero, so these priors also allow sparsity, where only a few entries are far from zero. Sparsity, non-negativity, and the simple bi-linear structure of the likelihood in HPF together give a simple interpretation of the model: in HPF a predictive density for each matrix element is formed from a linear combination of a subset of representation elements, and the elements of \mathbf{B} determine the relative additive contributions of each of the elements (Fig. 1 a). However, how each latent factor is composed in terms of the original items is not explicitly determined, it comes out of Bayesian inference (Fig. 1 c).

## 1.4 Limitations of HPF

Classical non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) is often said to have a column-clustering property, where the data features are grouped into coherent factors. The standard HPF of Eq. 1 does not have this property. In HPF each prediction is a linear combination of a subset of factors, but each factor is not necessarily a linear combination of a subset of features (shown in Fig. 1 c).

The transformation matrix \mathbf{B} defines a decoder (Def. 2) like a classic autoencoder. But a corresponding encoding transformation (Def. 1) does not explicitly appear in the formulation of Eq. 1. To determine the composition of the factors it is not enough to just read the decoding matrix row-wise. Mathematically, sparsity in decoding does not imply sparsity in encoding, in the same way that pseudo-inverses of sparse matrices are not necessarily sparse.

HPF also can not perform feature selection. By Eq. 1, predictions are formed by weighting representations with values from columns of the decoding matrix – the terms of a feature in the decoding matrix will be near zero if and only if the mean of that feature is near zero. If a feature column is excluded from the decoding matrix, that gives no information on whether the feature plays a part in generating representations. This deficiency can also make HPF wrongly imply structure when there is none, as shown in Fig. 3 a) on a factorization of pure Poisson noise.

## 1.5 Our contributions

We propose a method that self-consistently constrains HPF so that its corresponding encoding transformation is explicit. This improves the interpretability of HPF, and it gives it the ability to perform feature selection. Constraining HPF like this also makes it more suitable for training with large datasets, because the representation matrix does not have to be stored in memory. With a medical claims case study, we show how our method makes it easier to reparameterize decision rules in representation space into corresponding rules on the original data features.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
For many inverse problems, such as those found in healthcare, model interpretability is paramount. Building interpretable solutions that also perform well is technically challenging and requires flexible frameworks. A general approach to these and other problems is to structure solutions into pipelines: by ensuring that each step in such a pipeline is interpretable, one can achieve interpretability of the overall larger model.

Data sources for natural language processing, medical informatics, and bioinformatics are often high-dimensional count matrices. A common first step in modeling high-dimensional data sets is to use dimensionality reduction to find tractable data representations (also called factors or embeddings), which are then fed into downstream analyses. Our goal is to develop a dimension reduction scheme for count matrices such that the reduced representation has an innate interpretation in terms of the original data features.

## 1.1 Interpretability versus explainability

We seek latent data representations that are not only post-hoc explainable [1,2] but also intrinsically interpretable [3]. Our definition of intrinsic interpretability requires that it is clear how the model outputs are computed from the original variables, and that the latent variables and interactions within the model are meaningful.

Post-hoc explanations are based on a subjective examination of a solution through the lens of subject-matter expertise. For black-box models lacking intrinsic interpretability, these explanations are produced using simpler approximating models (typically local linear regressions). Besides being inexact, such explanations can also be misleading [1]. Examples of black-box models relying on approximation techniques for explainability are found throughout the deep learning literature.

## 1.2 Disentangled autoencoders

Disentangled variational autoencoders [4,5,6] are deep learning models that are inherently mindful of post-hoc model explainability. Like other autoencoders, these models have an encoder-decoder structure (see Definitions 1 and 2), where the encoder generates dimensionally reduced representations.

The encoder transformation maps input data features to latent representations

The decoder transformation maps latent representations to predictions

Disentangled autoencoders use a combination of penalties [4,7] and structural constraints [8] to encourage statistical independence in representations, which facilitates explanation. These methods arose in computer vision and have demonstrated empirical utility in producing nonlinear factor models whose factors are conceptually sensible. Yet, due to the black-box nature of deep learning, explanations of how the factors are generated from the data, using local saliency maps for instance, are unreliable or imprecise [1,9,10]. In imaging applications, where the features are raw pixels, this type of interpretability is unnecessary. When modeling structured data problems, however, one often wishes to learn the effects of the individual data features.

## 1.3 Probabilistic matrix factorization

Probabilistic matrix factorization methods are related to autoencoders [11] and are often presented in the context of recommender systems. In these cases, rows of the input matrix are attributed to users and columns (features) to items. Probabilistic matrix factorization methods are bi-linear in item- and user-specific effects, de-convolving them in a manner similar to item response theory [12]. In applications with non-negative data, non-negative sparse matrix factorization methods further improve interpretability by computing predictions using only additive terms [13].

For count matrices, [14] introduced hierarchical Poisson matrix factorization (HPF). Suppose \mathbf{Y}=(y_{ui}) is a U\times I matrix of non-negative integers, where each row corresponds to a user and each column to an item (feature). Adopting their notation, [14] formulated their model as

where \bm{\Theta}=(\theta_{uk}) is a U\times K matrix, and \mathbf{B}=(\beta_{ki}) is the representation decoder matrix. Additional priors \eta_{i}\sim\textrm{Gamma}(c^{\prime},c^{\prime}/d^{\prime}) and \xi_{u}\sim\textrm{Gamma}(a^{\prime},a^{\prime}/b^{\prime}) model item and user-specific variability in the dataset, and a^{\prime},b^{\prime},c^{\prime},d^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{+} are hyper-parameters. The row vector \bm{\theta}_{u}=(\theta_{u1},\ldots,\theta_{uK}) constitutes a K -dimensional representation of the user, and the matrix \mathbf{B}=(\beta_{ki}) decodes the representation into predictions of the user's counts.

In HPF, the gamma priors on the decoder matrix \mathbf{B}=(\beta_{ki}) enforce non-negativity. Because the gamma distribution can have density at zero, these priors also allow for sparsity, where only a few of the entries are far from zero. Sparsity, non-negativity, and the simple bi-linear structure of the likelihood in HPF combine to yield a simple interpretation of the model: a predictive density for each matrix element is formed using a linear combination of a subset of representation elements, where the elements of \mathbf{B} determine the relative additive contributions of each element (Fig. 1 a). However, the composition of each latent factor in terms of the original items is not explicitly determined; it arises from Bayesian inference (Fig. 1 c).

## 1.4 Limitations of HPF

Classical non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) is often touted for its column-clustering property [15], where data features are grouped into coherent factors. The standard HPF of Eq. 1 lacks this property: while each prediction is a linear combination of a subset of factors, each factor is not necessarily a linear combination of a subset of features (depicted in Fig. 1 c).

The transformation matrix \mathbf{B} defines a decoder (Def. 2), as in a classic autoencoder, but a corresponding encoding transformation (Def. 1) does not explicitly appear in the formulation of Eq. 1. Determining the composition of factors is not simply a matter of reading the decoding matrix row-wise. Mathematically, sparsity in decoding does not imply sparsity in encoding, analogous to how pseudo-inverses of sparse matrices are not necessarily sparse.

HPF is also unable to perform feature selection. By Eq. 1, predictions are formed by weighting representations using values from columns of the decoding matrix – a feature's corresponding terms in the decoding matrix will be near zero if and only if that feature's mean is near zero. Excluding a feature column from the decoding matrix therefore yields no information on whether that feature plays a part in generating representations. This deficiency can also cause HPF to erroneously imply structure when none is present, as demonstrated in Fig. 3 a) on a factorization of pure Poisson noise.

## 1.5 Our contributions

We propose a method to self-consistently constrain HPF so that its corresponding encoding transformation is explicit. In doing so, we improve the interpretability of HPF and give it the ability to perform feature selection. Constraining HPF in this manner also makes it more suitable for training with large datasets, because the representation matrix need not be stored in memory. Using a medical claims case study, we demonstrate how our method facilitates reparameterization of decision rules in representation space into corresponding rules on the original data features.
